The claim states that casting rays from the image plane causes voxels to be 'missed or double-counted'. However, the evidence in Source [S3] and Source [S4] explicitly states the opposite. Both sources describe a method where rays are emitted from a plane parallel to the volume faces (the image plane/base-plane) and assert that this specific placement 'guarantees complete and uniform tessellation of the volume' and 'uniform sampling'. The evidence supports the claim that this method avoids missing or double-counting voxels, thereby contradicting the claim.

The base image $I_{base}$ is geometrically distorted relative to the final image because it was generated on a plane parallel to the volume face, not the image plane [S4, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S4] explicitly states that the algorithm chooses a 'base-plane' which is 'parallel to one of the volume faces'. It further explains that the image is computed by sliding the template along this base-plane and that the final step involves mapping the projected image from the base-plane onto the screen-plane (image plane) using a 2D image transformation. This process implies that the base image (generated on the base-plane) is geometrically distinct from the final image (on the screen-plane) due to the projection/transformation required to map between the plane parallel to the volume face and the screen plane.
